groups.title: Can a model score here without knowing the facts?

blocks.p: Always choosing the first option scores 68%, above every decision setup without search here. Answer-position and yes/true imbalances complicate the ranking; these checks cannot establish whether a model has seen the questions.

The right answer is the first choice on 68 questions, the second on 26, the third on 5 and the fourth on 1. 60 questions are yes/no (53) or true/false (7); on every one "yes" or "true" is the first choice, and "yes" or "true" is right on 48 of them (42 of 53 and 6 of 7). The checks below use only totals: the answer key's positions, each decision setup's answers over its 3 runs, and public dates.

blocks.li: Shares are of each setup's answers over its 3 runs. The habit baseline is the score of a strategy that never reads the question but has the setup's habits, by number of choices: on the 60 yes/no and true/false questions it says "yes" or "true" as often as the setup does there; on the other 17 two-choice questions it picks the first choice as often as the setup does on them; on three- and four-choice questions it picks each position as often as the setup does on questions of that size. "Above the habits" is accuracy minus that baseline.

The p values are exploratory, not a validated test: the one-sided chance that the habit strategy, answering each question independently, scores at least the setup's mean accuracy, by a normal approximation with the variance of one run of 100 questions (the habits come from the same answers and are treated as known; the 3 runs of the same questions are not independent). Holm's correction over the 37 setups without search: lowest adjusted p 0.48. Across those 37, the share of first-choice answers and accuracy correlate at r = 0.93.

"At or below habit baseline + 1 pt" marks the 9 setups whose accuracy is below their habit baseline or at most 1 point above it (a one-sided rule: no lower limit). It is a descriptive threshold: a score at or below that line is consistent with the habits, not proof that they cause it. The setup with web search never gets the mark. The ranking's note beside these setups gives their first-choice share over all 100 questions; since "yes" or "true" is always the first choice, that share mixes the "yes" habit with a pure position habit. The two columns before the baseline separate them.

12 decision setups without search answered the 100 questions once more with each question's choices in reverse order, each answer mapped back to the original choice before scoring; the main scores and the ranking are unchanged. 9 of the 12 scored within 3 points of their run 1; Strands Decider 2B (-10.0), REAX 1.3 (-8.0) and d1-ultra (-4.0) scored more than 3 points lower, consistent with sensitivity to the position of the choices.

blocks.p: Earliest public records of the questions we can observe: the Hugging Face dataset parallel-web/pws-decisions-benchmark was created on 1 November 2026 at 23:49 UTC; its only commit, 64da0d8, of 2 November 2026 at 01:37 UTC, holds the questions. The GitHub repository's only commit, 0f403cf, of 2 November 2026 at 17:33 UTC, holds none. All but one of the 21 open setups' revisions were committed 3 to 105 days before; the revision of REAX 1.3 was committed 1 day after (commit dates as the Hugging Face API gave them, read 6 November 2026; files can be older). A revision's commit date is not the end of its training, which no maker here states, so the order of these dates shows neither use nor absence of use of the questions. These dates do not rule out earlier exposure to the questions or their sources; the API setups' training dates are unknown.

Cost: an estimate, each run's recorded tokens at the runner's list price for the setup, the price the Text tab uses, over its 100 questions, plus the web search fee for setups with web ($0.001 per request for Perplexity). It is not a provider's bill: an API usage cost estimate for a run through an API key, an API-equivalent estimate for a run through a subscription, a list-price estimate for a model on our GPU. Where a fee is missing from the estimate, the setup's row says so.
A line under a name, “picks the first choice in N of 10 questions; …”: that setup scores at most 1 point above what its answering habits alone would score (without knowing the facts).

groups.title: Our method

blocks.p: Each question went out as PWS-Decisions' own request (its state, and one choice question with its instructions and its choices), with the setup's model name, to the same API and endpoint as the setup's Text tab run. OpenAI's Decisions API takes the same parts under its own names. One question per request, each provider's requests one after another, the providers at the same time. Timeout 60 s; the runner's retries (up to 5, on 408, 425, 429 and 5xx, and transport failures). Scored with PWS-Decisions' own scorer: a refusal, an error or an invalid answer counts as wrong.

blocks.li: Request time: from sending a request to its answer, retries included, over the requests that got an answer; the median and the 95th percentile by nearest rank.
The chance line, 44.67%: the mean over the 100 questions of 1 / the number of choices, (77 × 1/2 + 5 × 1/3 + 18 × 1/4) / 100.

The 95% interval: 10,000 resamples of the 100 questions with replacement (seed 20261105), each question scored as the mean of its 3 runs' correctness (a missing answer is wrong); the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the resampled accuracy. It is the uncertainty from the question sample; the lowest to highest run is the run-to-run range.
d1 was asked as d1: Liquid's API no longer serves the d1:free name of its Text tab run.

Perplexity's own figures: 86% with web on these questions, with 370 ms at the median and 685 ms at the 95th percentile from Perplexity's client (Web grounding for the Decisions API, 4 November 2026); the 51% without is Parallel's leaderboard figure.

Parallel's leaderboard (public set, mean of three runs, evaluated 29 October 2026): Parallel Decisions API (fast) 78.33%; Perplexity Decisions (pplx-decider-v1.2, through OpenRouter) 51.00%; OpenAI Decisions API (gpt-6-luna) 42.00%; Baseten Mammoth (baseten-mammoth-27b-latest) 37.00%; TypeSafe Jev 1.14 (jev-1.14.0) 33.33% (the benchmark's repository).
The questions and answers are Parallel's: PWS-Decisions version 0.1.0-rc1, gated, for evaluation only. We publish totals only, never a question, an answer or a per-question result.
The runs' API usage cost estimate at list prices (subscription runs as API-equivalent estimates): $258; not a provider's bill.
